abstract: Impaired wound repair is a major complication of diabetes, yet how microbiota-derived metabolites sustain inflammation remains unclear. By integrating metabolomic and microbiome profiling of individuals with type 2 diabetes, we identify phenylethylamine as an elevated microbiota-associated metabolite. In mouse cutaneous and oral wounds, phenylethylamine promotes neutrophil extracellular trap formation and delays wound healing. Mechanistically, phenylethylamine signals through trace amine-associated receptor 1 on neutrophils, engaging β-arrestin-extracellular signal-regulated kinase-reactive oxygen species signaling. Microbiota depletion lowers circulating phenylethylamine, whereas Enterococcus faecalis recolonization increases its concentration and delays repair, supporting a microbial contribution to phenylethylamine exposure. Local delivery of a receptor antagonist in a thermosensitive hydrogel reduces neutrophil extracellular traps and improves cutaneous and oral healing in diabetic mice. These findings provide preclinical support for local TAAR1 blockade as a potential approach to improving diabetic wound repair.
